Shegaga. Iron hoe, triangular head, straight blade with sloping sides meeting at an open cylindrical socket.

Gadum. Adze, sometimes used for hollowing Poto drums, with a wooden handle that bends at a right angle. The straight-edged metal blade is attached to the bend at the top of the handle with flanges. The wood of the handle has cracked in several places.

Dunger Shāl. Bird trap consisting of a long narrow, slightly curved stick, with a socketed metal loop and a small wooden pointed peg secured by fibre at one end. Described on the catalogue card as a 'Springe trap...bird trap for doves and other small birds'.

Taka Gīri. Bird trap. Bundle of one long slightly curved stick, a cane mat, a looped stick secured by plant fibre and two lengths of string. Attached to the small length of string is a small pointed stick. Described on the catalogue card as a 'Spinge trap...for catching Dīk el Hol and other night feeding birds'.

Sungeram. Hare trap. Attached at one end of the long curved stick is a bundle of two scorched hollow wooden sticks. At the opposing end is an attached bundle of five wooden sticks, a socketed metal loop and a wooden peg attached to a mud-coated string which extends up to the middle of the curved stick. Described on the catalogue card as a 'springe trap'.
Tultu. Kudu hunting horn, blown to claim game. The horn is spiralled, with ridges along the edge. There is a hole approximately halfway along the horn.
Gourd cup used to fill a spouted gourd (Nishaga) with heglig oil. Cup is made from half of a small, undecorated, circular gourd.

Umra. Basket used for water or food. The basket has a rounded base, and is decorated with chevrons of hide. The lid has an upturned rim, and is attached to the body of the basked with  a looped handle threaded around the plaited hide handle.

Rakwa. Clay water pot, with a small spout, an opening, with a handle in between. The opening has a flat projecting rim and circular neck. The body is oval in shape, with a footring base. Twisted cord tied the small handle, used for carrying.

Sakhana. Round-bodied pot of red fabric with wide, cylindrical neck and open mouth; everted rim. Two looped handles at join between neck and body. A smooth coat has been applied to the upper two thirds.

Diro Diro. Spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped with a wide midrib and collar below the shoulder. The socket is decorated with pairs of grooves. The shaft has a circular cross-section, with a coil of metal at the terminal.
Tirit. Boys spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is short and leaf shaped, with a split socket. The shaft has a circular cross-section.

Double spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is double, each with one straight edge and one curved, with two ribs on the surface of the blade. The shank has a flat cross-section, decorated with grooves and zigzags; split socket with a circular cross-section. The shaft has a circular cross-section.

Knife and sheath. The knife (.1) has a dark wooden handle with a disc at the end. The sheather (.2) is made from brown leather with three sections of reptile skin and a black leather tip. The brown leather is decorated on one side with geometric diamond pattern and on the other side with three raised ridges. Attached to the top of the sheath is a twisted looped leather handle. Made by Tama from spring of motor car. Blade cannot be separated from sheath.
Elephant hunter's knife with iron blade and wooden handle. Long, double-edged blade with slight mid-rib; tang set into a wooden handle which flares towards the butt. Tip broken and missing.

Large flat sword. The blade is rectangular with a short point at one end and a narrow handle with a triangular terminal. Wrapped around the handle are blue and beige cotton fabric strips. Made from a Ford spring.
Knife, iron blade decorated with incised horizontal lines and central 'X' pattern. The handle is made from iron but wrapped into hide and sewn with cotton thread. The binding is coming undone.

Mirmirita. Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is short and leaf shaped with a midrib. The shank has a circular, spiralled cross-section; socket with a short split with edges meeting. The shaft has a circular cross-section with a coil of metal around the terminal.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped with a midrib; the shank has a squared cross-section with short barbs on both edges; split socket with edges meeting. The shaft has a circular cross-section with a coil of metal midway up, and a coil of metal around the terminal.

Knife and sheath. The knife (.1) has a wooden handle with an oval cross-section that flares at both ends. The blade is iron and straight along both sides. The sheath (.2) is made from sections of leather with a reptile skin tip. Attached to the top of the sheath is a twisted leather handle that is becoming unwound.

Wier Kait. Throwing spear for boys with a wooden shaft and metal blade. The blade is short and leaf shaped, with a slightly rounded tip; the blade has faint grooves around the outside edge and a long split socket. The shaft has a circular cross-section and a slightly tapered terminal.

Spear with a wooden shaft and metal point. The spearhead is a large point with circular cross-section, with a protruding square shank. The split socket is short with edges meeting. Long shaft of dark wood with a circular cross-section and bound at the terminal with a strip of hide.

Spear with a wooden shaft and pointed spearhead. Spearhead terminates in a short point; the shank has a rectangular cross-section decorated with small dashes, and with downward facing barbs on both edges. Split socket decorated one third of the way down with a lozenge shaped projection decorated with grooves. The shaft has a circular cross-section and tapers slightly towards the terminal.

Spear with wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is narrow and leaf shaped, and decorated with pairs of grooves following the outside edge. The shank has a flattened cross-section, and is decorated with off centre cross-hatching and grooves with curved barbs on either side. Between the shank and socket is a oval and rectangular sections both decorated with grooves; socket is also decorated with cross-hatching and grooves. The shaft has a circular cross-section, with a coil of metal around the terminal.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is long and leaf shaped with a midrib and grooves along the outside edges. The shank has a rectangular cross-section decorated with cross-hatching and short barbs along the outside edges; split socket with a circular cross-section. The shaft has a circular cross-section, with a coil of metal around the terminal.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is small and leaf shaped, with a faint midrib and grooves following the outside edges; below the shoulders are two downward pointing barbs. The shank has a rectangular cross-section decorated with cross-hatching and grooves, with barbs down all edges. The socket has a geometric section near the centre, decorated with grooves. The shaft has a circular cross section.

Am Tun; Derib Ma Fi. Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is narrow and angular with a faint midrib and barbs below the shoulders. The shank has a circular cross section, and is decorated with transverse grooves; two barbs pointing different directions on the shank. The socket ha a geometric section decorated with grooves. Shaft has a circular cross-section.

Surat el Meiram. Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped, with midrib and ridges following the outside edge. The socket has a circular cross section and is decorated at the top with chevrons and grooves. The shaft has a circular cross-section. Used by Sultan Ali Dinar and his relatives.

Tabaga. Spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is large and leaf shaped, with a midrib, ridges that follow the outside edge and decorated with a few grooves. Split socket, with cloth at the base. The shaft has a circular cross-section.

masks-ritual.title: Double incense burner of red ware pottery. Two bowls, each with a band of perforations, on two conical feet, attached by a bridge between the pedestals and a smaller one between the bowls. Over each bowl are three arches, these two sets of arches are then connected by a flat bridge on top of which is a small saucer. The arches are decorated with a (faded) graphite paint and decorated with incised chevrons. [MOBB [OPS move] 30/06/2016]

Masha. A pair of smith's tongs used for charcoal. They are forged from a single piece of metal that has been folded in the middle. There is a loop at the central bend, and the arms are 'S' shaped at the open end. Possibly used together with D 1937.148 B.
Small egg-shaped stone, used for smoothing pots. It has two small circular grooves on the surface.
Khokha. Cotton seed gin. 'Y' shaped wooden frame with singly-branched sticks inserted across the 'V' and wedged with pieces of cotton cloth and strips of bark.

Beitiga. A pair of smith's tongs, made from two pieces of metal. The two pieces are connected by a rivet around three quarters of the way along, that allows the tongs to open and close. On the longer side (the handle), the arms are cylindrical at the top, but have been flattened close to rivet. On the shorter side, the arms have a slight convex curve, the straighten out at the end. Possibly used with D 1937.148 A.
